question: What is the meaning of resource consumption in relation to manufacturing data?
description: Resource consumption in relation to manufacturing data refers to the utilization of raw materials, feedstock, or components to create physical products or their elements. It involves tracking the origin, treatment, usage, and final destination of materials throughout their lifecycle. This information is crucial for understanding the environmental impact, optimizing resource efficiency, and supporting recycling or repurposing efforts in a circular economy. The patterns and modules described in the text, such as 'Name Stub', 'Identifier', 'Explicit Typing', 'Provenance', and 'AgentRole', are used to capture and model this information systematically.

These data points are directly related and imperative to the assessment 
of a product's condition and suitability for reuse (Addis, 2006) and also 
were included in the many reviewed MP approaches (see Supplementary 
Materials). Therefore, our findings confirm the previous approaches that 
included these data points (e.g., BAMB (2019); G¨oswein et al. (2022); 
(BAMB, 2019; G¨oswein et al., 2022); Munaro and Tavares (2021)). 
Among the five product data categories (B to F), “C-Product Prop­
erties” and “F-Product End-of-Life Aspects” seem to be critical to meet 
users' data requirements, while many of the data points included under 
“E-Product Operational Aspects” are assigned to be “nice-to-have”. 
There could be several reasons for this trend. First, categories C and F 
support reuse and recycle strategies, thus, closing the material loops, 
while category E is, to a large extent, related to expanding the life cycle 
of products, so slowing the material loops. MPs, therefore, are seen as 
tools for circularity at the end-of-life by the practitioners rather than a 
whole life cycle data solution as proposed by researchers (Aguiar et al., 
2019; G¨oswein et al., 2022; Munaro and Tavares, 2021). Another reason 
could be that maintenance activities, although maintenance itself is a 
circular strategy, are not yet fully operationalised through circular 
material flows by social housing organisations. Therefore, the link be­
tween the use and end-of-use phases of products is not explicitly made in 
terms of data management. The empirical findings of Çetin et al. (2022) 
support this, as their multiple-case study with three social housing or­
ganisations also showed that practitioners tend to see MPs as an end-of- 
life tool due to the difficulties in managing life cycle data for a long time. 
However, though, as some interviewees mentioned, the maintenance log 
of a product could be a fruitful source of data when deciding on end-of- 
life treatment options. 
There are modest differences between the data requirements of 
housing professionals (Fig. 6(a)) and identified potential users (Fig. 6 
(b)). Three data points, namely, “Building energy label” (A.06), 
“Drawings and BIM model” (B.18), and “Cleaning instructions” (F.35), 
seem to be insignificant for the potential external users while many 
interviewed housing professionals perceive them as nice-to-have. A 
possible explanation for this could be that the majority of the third- 
round interviewees (nine out of ten) have expertise in reuse practices 
(e.g., harvesting, design, and consultancy), and these three data points 
do not directly impact their decisions in reusing products. For example, 
one interviewee from a reuse company noted that they need to inspect 
the donor building for the identification of reclaimable products, 
whether they have drawings and maintenance or cleaning instructions 
or not. Building products are subject to changes throughout their life­
time, and condition assessment needs to be performed on the location 
even though the building is fully documented.

4.3.3.1.2. Material. The term ‘resource’, as it is defined in ISO/DIS 
59004, is synonymous with “raw material”, “feedstock”, “material” or 
“component. In this context, the definition of resource is adopted for our 
‘Material’ key notion, which is an “asset from which a solution is created or 
implemented”. This standard defines solution as “product, service or a 
combination thereof, that fulfills a need”. We aligned our ‘Material’ key 
notion with the MAT's Material defined as “a homogeneous or inhomo­
geneous substance that can be used to form elements (physical products or 
their components.” Given the broad scope of the material definition we 
adopted from the ISO/DIS 59904, we introduced the mat:Material from 
MAT as a specialization of our ‘Material’ key notion. Table 7 provides the 
summary of how our ‘Material’ key notion aligns with Material from 
MAT. 
Following the IRs identified from literature and interviews, and the 
EC proposals for DPPs, the material module we introduced incorporates 
properties, relationships, and attributes associated with different types 
of materials. We started by first employing the ‘Name Stub’ and ‘Identi­
fier’ modules to identify materials by their names and unique identifiers 
(see Fig. 8). 
‘Explicit Typing’ pattern is selected to capture information related to 
the types or categories of materials such as metal, plastic or composite. 
This pattern allows for more straightforward classification and querying. 
It can also be used to categorize various types of material properties such 
as mechanical, chemical, etc., without the need to create a large number 
of subclasses (see Fig. 7). 
Tracking the lifecycle of materials is crucial for a circular economy. 
The ‘Provenance’ pattern enables to track materials by keeping record of 
their origin, how they have been treated and used, and where they end 
up. This is critical information for recycling or repurposing of materials. 
To capture the provenance information, we introduced the Material 
class as a specialized version of “EntityWithProvenance”. With this 
pattern, we can capture information about how the material is made 
using the ‘generatedBy’ property and who is responsible for the creating 
or manufacturing the material using the ‘attributedTo’ property. Using 
the ‘used’ property, we can indicate that something was utilized in the 
process of creating something else, in our case, what materials or com­
ponents were involved in making a final product. Additionally, the 
‘wasDerivedFrom’ makes it possible to model the historical context of 
materials by capturing information about from where or what the ma­
terial is originated from. The ‘AgentRole’ pattern also provides more 
context to model information related to agents and the roles they play to 
create and use materials along with the temporal information. Infor­
